Graph & Geometric Deep Learning
for Drug Toxicity Prediction

Can models that read molecular structure directly beat classical fingerprint baselines at predicting toxicity — and does the answer depend on the task?
Konstantina Paschou  ·  Georgios Kesoglidis  ·  Theocharis Angelidis Supervisor  Prof. Grigorios Tsoumakas

Classical leads on paper — but every GNN scores negative R² under scaffold splits. A leakage signal, not a real win (Panel 4A).

1
The StudyFour representation families, one fair benchmark

Molecules are graphs: atoms are nodes, bonds are edges. We ask whether learning directly on that structure — in 2D or 3D — outperforms hand-crafted fingerprints across toxicity endpoints of differing size and balance.

Classical
Random Forest, XGBoost on Morgan fingerprints (ECFP4, 1024-bit)
Language
ChemBERTa — frozen RoBERTa pre-trained on 77M SMILES + linear head
GNN · 2D
GCN, GIN, GAT, GraphSAGE, GINE — graph topology; GINE adds bond features
GNN · 3D
SchNet on RDKit ETKDG 3D conformer geometry
Datasets  5 TDC toxicity tasks (DILI, ClinTox, AMES, hERG, LD50) + the 12-endpoint Tox21 panel.  Protocol  Bemis–Murcko scaffold splits (structurally disjoint train/test), 3 seeds, 70/10/20, class-weighted loss.  Metric  AUROC, or R² for LD50.
2
Main Result — the winner depends on the taskBest GNN minus best classical AUROC, per dataset

A consistent split emerges. GNNs win on the hard cases — small, imbalanced datasets such as DILI (n=475) and ClinTox (8% positive), where learning structure-aware representations pays off. Classical fingerprints win on the large, balanced cases — AMES and hERG — where reactive substructures are common and a fingerprint already captures the decisive signal.

No single method dominates. Architecture choice should follow dataset size, class balance and chemistry — not a default preference for the newest model.
3
Full Benchmark — 8 methods × 5 datasetsAUROC, mean over 3 scaffold-split seeds (R² for LD50) · bold = best per column · † = std > 0.03

No universal winner. GIN and GINE top the imbalanced classification tasks; RF and XGBoost top the balanced ones.

  • ChemBERTa finishes last on every classification dataset despite 77M-molecule pre-training — frozen SMILES features do not transfer to unseen scaffolds.
  • GIN tops two endpoints (ClinTox 0.820, DILI 0.870); GINE's bond features add a further edge on DILI (0.860) and hERG.
  • Every GNN scores negative R² on LD50 regression under scaffold splits — foreshadowing the leakage finding below.
Pre-training is not a shortcut. Under a realistic generalisation test, a 500-tree Random Forest on fingerprints beats a 77M-parameter language model on all four classification tasks.
4A
LD50 — a leakage cautionary tale

Under random splits GIN looks strong (R²≈0.49). Under scaffold splits every GNN collapses below zero — GIN −0.52, GINE −0.76.

Random-split LD50 measures memorisation, not prediction. The widely cited R²≈0.49 for GNNs is data leakage.
4B
Does 3D geometry help?

SchNet (3D conformers) never beats GINE (2D + bonds) on any seed; the gap narrows from 0.10 on ClinTox to 0.017 on AMES as data grows.

3D buys uncertainty, not accuracy. Prediction spread across conformers reliably flags unreliable molecules — a free, post-hoc reliability signal.
4C
Multi-task Tox21

One shared GIN backbone across all 12 Tox21 endpoints vs 12 single-task models. Macro-average AUROC drops by 0.024; only a few related receptors (NR-AR-LBD, SR-ATAD5) benefit.

Forced sharing hurts. The 12 pathways are too biologically diverse to share one representation.
★
Conclusions
1
The winner depends on the task. GNNs lead on hard, imbalanced datasets; classical fingerprints lead on large, balanced ones. No single method dominates.
2
LD50 benchmarks can mislead. Scaffold splits expose near-zero generalisation; the widely cited R²≈0.49 for GNNs is data leakage.
3
3D geometry buys uncertainty, not accuracy. SchNet trails GINE on every seed, but conformer variance flags unreliable predictions for free.
4
Evaluation protocol changes the story. Multi-task transfer hurts, frozen ChemBERTa underperforms, and random-split results cannot be trusted — scaffold splitting is essential.

Setup & Reproducibility

RDKit featurisation · PyTorch Geometric · scikit-learn / XGBoost. All runs use a shared Murcko scaffold splitter for cross-method comparability; per-run weights and metrics are checkpointed for resumability.
